summary: This experimental document defines the bundle security protocol for the Delay-Tolerant Networking Bundle Protocol. It provides integrity and confidentiality, with separate protection for the payload and additional data. It also discusses security considerations and policy options.

plainLanguage.summary: Parcels moving through slow networks need locks and seals. This explains how to lock the contents and seal the labels in a DTN bundle.

subtitle: Four security blocks that protect bundles hop by hop or end to end in delay-tolerant networks.

tldr.problem: Bundles in delay-tolerant networks cross stressed, partly untrusted links and need protection, with different treatment for the payload and for other blocks.
tldr.mechanism: The Bundle Security Protocol adds four block types: BAB for hop-by-hop authentication, PIB for payload integrity, PCB for payload confidentiality and ESB for other blocks. Ciphersuites decide the algorithms, and blocks are added and removed like a stack.
tldr.outcome: It defines one mandatory ciphersuite per block type, using HMAC, RSA with SHA-256 and AES-GCM, and leaves key management largely to others. It is an Experimental document from the IRTF.

today: RFC 6257 is an Experimental document from the IRTF, published in May 2011. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Securing the Bundle Protocol
sections.content:
Delay-tolerant networks (DTNs) run over stressed links, and part of the network may be compromised, so confidentiality, integrity and availability all matter. This RFC defines the Bundle Security Protocol (BSP) for the DTN Bundle Protocol, plus a set of mandatory ciphersuites, which are specific bundles of algorithms and rules.

BSP applies only at security-aware nodes. Other nodes simply relay the security blocks unchanged. The RFC also defines the roles of a security-source, which adds a block, and a security-destination, which processes it. The two can differ from the bundle's own source and destination, so protection paths for different blocks can differ.
sections.plainLanguage: Some of the helpers who pass a parcel along may not know the secret rules. The ones who do know add and check seals, and the rest just pass the parcel on.

sections.title: The Four Security Blocks
sections.content:
A bundle may carry four kinds of security block. The Bundle Authentication Block (BAB) protects authenticity and integrity across one hop between security-aware nodes. The Payload Integrity Block (PIB) protects the payload from its security-source to its security-destination. The Payload Confidentiality Block (PCB) says the payload was encrypted. The Extension Security Block (ESB) protects non-payload blocks, never the primary block, the payload, or PIBs and PCBs.

When a BAB is present it MUST be the outer layer, calculated and added after all other security blocks. Several related blocks can be tied together by a correlator, for example a BAB at the front carrying the ciphersuite details and another at the end carrying the MAC, so a memory-limited node can verify without buffering everything.
sections.plainLanguage: There are four kinds of stickers. One says the last carrier is genuine, one says the contents were not changed, one says the contents are locked, and one locks the little notes on the side.

sections.title: The Abstract Security Block
sections.content:
All four blocks share one layout, described as an abstract security block (ASB). It is only a specification device, and no bundle contains an actual ASB. Numeric fields use the SDNV (Self-Delimiting Numeric Value) type from the Bundle Protocol. The fields are the block type, processing flags, an optional EID-reference list, the block data length, a ciphersuite ID, ciphersuite flags, an optional correlator, optional ciphersuite parameters and an optional security result.

The five ciphersuite flags say which optional parts are present: source EID reference, destination EID reference, parameters, correlator and result. Parameters and results are made of type-length-value items such as an initialization vector, key information, a fragment range, an integrity signature, a salt, an integrity check value and an encapsulated block.
sections.plainLanguage: All four stickers use the same form with boxes to fill in. Some boxes stay empty when they are not needed.

sections.title: Processing Order and Security Regions
sections.content:
Order matters. Security blocks are added and removed in last-in-first-out order, like a stack placed right after the primary block. The destination undoes actions in the reverse of the order the source applied them, which is why forwarding nodes MUST NOT reorder blocks. A BAB is always pushed last and stripped at the next security-aware hop, where a new BAB MAY be added.

This design cannot handle security paths that overlap partially. For instance, if BN1 protects for BN3 and BN2 adds protection for BN4, BN3 cannot remove the first block without breaking the second. Policies should therefore avoid naming a security-destination further away than an existing one.

Every node enforces its own security policy. If no policy is given, the default requires the mandatory ciphersuites, requires a valid BAB on every received bundle and adds one before forwarding, and does not add PIBs or PCBs.
sections.plainLanguage: Like putting on layers of wrapping paper, the last layer on is the first one taken off. Mixing up the order would leave a layer nobody can open.

sections.title: Mandatory Ciphersuites
sections.content:
Four ciphersuites are mandatory, one for each block type. BAB-HMAC (ID 0x001) uses HMAC-SHA1 over the strictly canonicalized bundle, with one BAB near the front and a correlated one at the end holding the result. PIB-RSA-SHA256 (ID 0x02) signs a canonical form of the bundle with RSA and SHA-256 using the CMS SignedData type.

PCB-RSA-AES128-PAYLOAD-PIB-PCB (ID 0x003) encrypts the payload in place with AES-128 in Galois/Counter Mode, which avoids growing the payload, and also encrypts any PIBs and PCBs. The random bundle encryption key travels RSA-encrypted in CMS enveloped data. ESB-RSA-AES128-EXT (ID 0x004) does the same for non-payload extension blocks.

Key management is largely left out. For testing, implementations SHOULD support well-known RSA public keys and pre-shared symmetric keys for BAB-HMAC.
sections.plainLanguage: The paper picks one standard lock for each kind of sticker, so any two helpers who follow it can open each other's locks.

sections.title: Security Considerations and Conformance
sections.content:
When both signing and encrypting, the order matters. Signing first and encrypting second proves who wrote the original plaintext. Signing the encrypted message lets intermediate nodes check it and cheaply reject bad bundles before costly decryption. The RFC recommends encrypt-then-sign as usually appropriate for a DTN.

The primary block, with the source and destination endpoint IDs, cannot be encrypted. Where that exposure matters, bundle-in-bundle encapsulation can be used. A PIB-destination that is not the final destination may verify a PIB en route, but the final destination cannot tell whether that happened. If a bundle is fragmented, all fragments must be reassembled before a PIB can be checked. Reports about failed checks may leak details of the network, so they should be generated with care.

A conformant implementation MUST support BSP and all four ciphersuites. One that supports fewer can claim only restricted compliance, and everyone is strongly RECOMMENDED to provide at least a BAB ciphersuite.
sections.plainLanguage: Locking the box and then signing the outside lets guards check the signature without opening the box. Signing the inside first proves who really packed it.
